variants.title: Move an event through the pipeline
variants.context: The pipeline moves an event through four stages: capture records it immutably with its source, schema version, event time, ingestion time, identity key, and consent context; validate quarantines contract violations with reason codes; transform applies one versioned point-in-time-safe definition; publish materializes offline and online views with the same feature names.
variants.prompt: A checkout event enters the platform for the first time and must reach both the training snapshot and the online store. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Validate the record against schema, freshness, uniqueness, and business constraints, quarantining violations with reason codes.
Publish the offline training snapshot and the low-latency online value under the same feature names and semantics.
Capture the event immutably with its source ID, schema version, event time, ingestion time, entity key, and consent context.
Transform the record with the one versioned, point-in-time-safe definition for windows, defaults, joins, and aggregations.

variants.hint: Which stage owns the raw record before anything is rewritten?
variants.explanation: Capture, validate, transform, publish. The raw event stays immutable so a later correction can replay from it.

variants.title: Move an event through the pipeline
variants.context: The pipeline moves an event through four stages: capture records it immutably with its source, schema version, event time, ingestion time, identity key, and consent context; validate quarantines contract violations with reason codes; transform applies one versioned point-in-time-safe definition; publish materializes offline and online views with the same feature names.
variants.prompt: A producer adds a new optional consent field to its payload. Put the steps in order for the stage-by-stage work the change creates.

items.text: Validation adds the field to the contract as an additive change and quarantines records whose consent context is unreadable.
Capture stores the new field with the bumped schema version alongside the untouched raw payload.
The transform reads the consent context inside the versioned feature definition rather than in ad hoc job code.
Publication ships the compatible feature version and records exactly which offline and online consumers moved.

variants.hint: The contract is checked before any feature value is computed.
variants.explanation: A schema change travels the same four stages. Additive fields pass the contract gate; the transform, not the job, decides what the field means.

variants.title: Move an event through the pipeline
variants.context: The pipeline moves an event through four stages: capture records it immutably with its source, schema version, event time, ingestion time, identity key, and consent context; validate quarantines contract violations with reason codes; transform applies one versioned point-in-time-safe definition; publish materializes offline and online views with the same feature names.
variants.prompt: A refund event arrives four hours after the purchase it corrects. Put the steps in order for how the pipeline handles it.

items.text: The transform recomputes the affected event-time window from the correct clock rather than from arrival order.
Capture keeps the refund with its true event time of 09:12 and its ingestion time of 13:20.
Validation confirms the late record still satisfies uniqueness and referential coverage before it is used.
Publication reissues the corrected offline snapshot and the online value so both paths agree again.

variants.hint: Which clock decides the window the refund belongs to?
variants.explanation: Late records keep their event time. Ingestion time only measures delay, so it must never define a historical window.

variants.title: Gate a publication
variants.context: Orchestration publishes only after validation. Plan the interval by pinning input partitions, event-time bounds, and schema and feature versions; write a candidate into an isolated location; validate and compare against the previous known-good version; then promote the compatible version atomically and record which consumers moved.
variants.prompt: A daily feature partition is being produced for the recommendation model. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Promote the compatible version atomically, retain lineage, and record which consumers moved.
Compute the result into an isolated staging version instead of the live serving view.
Run contracts, row counts, distribution checks, and offline and online parity checks against the previous known-good version.
Pin the input partitions, event-time bounds, schema and feature versions, and the target consumer.

variants.hint: Nothing reaches a serving view while validation is still incomplete.
variants.explanation: Scope, build, gate, release. Writing into the serving view before the gate removes the option to reject the candidate.

variants.title: Gate a publication
variants.context: Orchestration publishes only after validation. Plan the interval by pinning input partitions, event-time bounds, and schema and feature versions; write a candidate into an isolated location; validate and compare against the previous known-good version; then promote the compatible version atomically and record which consumers moved.
variants.prompt: A duplicate-event defect corrupted three days of a 30-day purchase feature. Put the backfill steps in order.

items.text: Recompute those days into an isolated version so the current serving view keeps answering.
Publish the repaired range atomically to both the training snapshot and the online materialization.
Scope the backfill to the smallest event-time range that repairs the defect, and pin the source and feature versions it needs.
Compare row counts, duplicate rate, and sampled feature values against the last known-good version.

variants.hint: Prefer the smallest range that actually repairs the error.
variants.explanation: A backfill follows the same gate. Both the training snapshot and the online store are repaired because the defect could otherwise create training-serving skew.

variants.title: Gate a publication
variants.context: Orchestration publishes only after validation. Plan the interval by pinning input partitions, event-time bounds, and schema and feature versions; write a candidate into an isolated location; validate and compare against the previous known-good version; then promote the compatible version atomically and record which consumers moved.
variants.prompt: A bad feature definition has already reached production. Put the deliberate recovery steps in order.

items.text: Preserve the raw inputs and checkpoints that explain what was produced.
Scope the bad event-time interval and the affected feature consumers.
Pause publication so no further corrupted values reach consumers.
Release the repaired version in a single reversible step.
Rebuild a candidate in an isolated version and validate it against the known-good release.

variants.hint: Stopping the bleeding comes before diagnosing the wound.
variants.explanation: Pause, preserve, scope, rebuild and validate, then release reversibly. Overwriting in place destroys the evidence the incident review needs.

variants.title: Pick the processing mode
variants.context: Choose the processing mode from the required freshness, not from a preferred tool. Batch suits hours of freshness and simple reproducible reruns. Streaming suits decisions that must change within seconds or minutes. Hybrid keeps a durable batch truth while a streaming path maintains recent state.
variants.prompt: A card-fraud control must block a suspicious authorization before the transaction completes, within a few seconds of the event. Which mode fits?
options: Streaming, because the event must change a decision within seconds.
Batch on a five-minute schedule, because the source already emits events.
Hybrid, because two paths are always safer than one.
optionFeedback: Correct: the freshness requirement is seconds, which only continuous evaluation can meet.
A five-minute schedule cannot meet a seconds-level decision deadline, and emitting events is not itself a reason to pick a mode.
Hybrid adds a second implementation with its own parity and operating cost, which this single seconds-level decision does not need.
variants.hint: Start from the freshness the decision requires.
variants.explanation: Streaming is justified by a decision deadline of seconds or minutes, not by the source format.

variants.title: Pick the processing mode
variants.context: Choose the processing mode from the required freshness, not from a preferred tool. Batch suits hours of freshness and simple reproducible reruns. Streaming suits decisions that must change within seconds or minutes. Hybrid keeps a durable batch truth while a streaming path maintains recent state.
variants.prompt: A churn model retrains weekly from a 90-day history. Hours of staleness are acceptable and large historical scans dominate the cost. Which mode fits?
options: Streaming, so the training features are always current to the second.
Hybrid, so a streaming path can maintain the 90-day aggregate.
Batch, because hours of freshness are acceptable and reruns must be simple.
optionFeedback: Streaming adds state, watermarks, late records, and checkpoint recovery for freshness this consumer never uses.
Maintaining a 90-day aggregate in stream state adds cost and replay risk without improving a weekly retrain.
Correct: bounded historical sets on a schedule give cheap scans and simple reproducible reruns.
variants.hint: What does the consumer actually lose if the data is four hours old?
variants.explanation: Batch is the default when the freshness SLO is hours, because reproducible reruns are cheaper than stream state.

variants.title: Pick the processing mode
variants.context: Choose the processing mode from the required freshness, not from a preferred tool. Batch suits hours of freshness and simple reproducible reruns. Streaming suits decisions that must change within seconds or minutes. Hybrid keeps a durable batch truth while a streaming path maintains recent state.
variants.prompt: Session recommendations need clicks from the last minute, while the same feature must be recomputable across two years for training and for corrections after a defect. Which mode fits?
options: Batch only, running the historical job every two minutes to approximate freshness.
Hybrid, keeping a durable batch truth while a streaming path maintains recent state.
Streaming only, retaining two years of events inside the stream processor state.
optionFeedback: A two-minute historical job repeats full scans and still misses the sub-minute requirement.
Correct: serving needs recent events while training and correction need a complete recomputable history.
Holding two years in stream state makes replay and recovery expensive and fragile.
variants.hint: Two different consumers can have two different deadlines.
variants.explanation: Hybrid is justified when one consumer needs seconds and another needs a complete recomputable history, accepting the parity cost.

variants.title: Read the event-time clocks
variants.context: Event time is when the business action happened and drives feature windows; ingestion time is when the platform received it and measures source delay. A watermark states an expected event-time position plus an allowed lateness, such as events through 10:00 allowing 15 minutes of lateness.
variants.prompt: A purchase happened at 09:55 and the platform received it at 10:07. How much source delay did this record experience?
variants.hint: Source delay is the gap between the two clocks, not a property of the window.
variants.explanation: Ingestion time minus event time measures source delay, which is what freshness monitoring watches.

mistakes.feedback: Subtracted the minute fields, 55 from 07, and ignored the hour rollover.
Measured only from 09:55 to the top of the hour and stopped at 10:00.

variants.title: Read the event-time clocks
variants.context: Event time is when the business action happened and drives feature windows; ingestion time is when the platform received it and measures source delay. A watermark states an expected event-time position plus an allowed lateness, such as events through 10:00 allowing 15 minutes of lateness.
variants.prompt: A window closes at event time 10:00 and the job allows 15 minutes of lateness. A record for that window is received at 10:19. By how many minutes did it miss the allowance boundary?
variants.hint: The boundary is the window close plus the allowance, not the window close.
variants.explanation: Allowed lateness moves the closing boundary forward, so a record is only late relative to that moved boundary. Records past it go to correction or replay.

mistakes.feedback: Measured against the window close at 10:00 instead of the 10:15 allowance boundary.
Reported the allowance itself rather than the amount by which it was exceeded.

variants.title: Read the event-time clocks
variants.context: Event time is when the business action happened and drives feature windows; ingestion time is when the platform received it and measures source delay. A watermark states an expected event-time position plus an allowed lateness, such as events through 10:00 allowing 15 minutes of lateness.
variants.prompt: A team lengthens allowed lateness from 10 minutes to 25 minutes to capture a delayed source. By how many minutes does a complete aggregate for each window now get postponed?
variants.hint: The trade-off is measured by the change in the allowance, not by its new size.
variants.explanation: A longer allowance improves correctness for delayed sources but postpones complete aggregates by exactly the extra wait.

mistakes.feedback: Reported the new allowance rather than the increase over the old one.
Added the two allowances instead of taking the difference.

variants.title: Sort the validation boundaries
variants.context: Contracts are validated at four boundaries. Schema covers required fields, types, allowed enumerations, and additive versus breaking changes. Quality covers null rate, numeric range, duplicate rate, referential coverage, and business invariants. Freshness covers source delay, partition completeness, stream lag, and online feature age. Distribution covers shifts in important feature values and slices.
variants.prompt: Match each validation boundary to what it checks.

pairs.label: Schema
pairs.detail: Required fields, types, allowed enumerations, and additive versus breaking changes.

pairs.label: Quality
pairs.detail: Null rate, numeric range, duplicate rate, referential coverage, and business invariants.

pairs.label: Freshness
pairs.detail: Maximum source delay, partition completeness, stream lag, and online feature age.

pairs.label: Distribution
pairs.detail: Shifts in important feature values and slices, read alongside product context.

variants.hint: One boundary asks whether the record parses, another whether its values are believable.
variants.explanation: Each boundary catches a different class of failure, so an aggregate quality score cannot substitute for running all four.

variants.prompt: Match each observed symptom to the validation boundary that should catch it.

pairs.label: The duplicate rate on the declared entity key rose to 4 percent
A producer began sending an enumeration value the contract never listed
The online feature age passed 40 minutes against a 10-minute target
Purchase amounts moved sharply for one region while volume held steady

variants.hint: Ask which contract statement each symptom violates.
variants.explanation: Routing a symptom to its boundary points at the owner and the recovery path instead of at a single red dashboard.

variants.title: Sort the validation boundaries
variants.context: Contracts are validated at four boundaries. Schema covers required fields, types, allowed enumerations, and additive versus breaking changes. Quality covers null rate, numeric range, duplicate rate, referential coverage, and business invariants. Freshness covers source delay, partition completeness, stream lag, and online feature age. Distribution covers shifts in important feature values and slices.
variants.prompt: A nightly run reports four findings. Match each finding to the validation boundary it belongs to.

pairs.label: Yesterday's partition is missing two of its twenty-four hourly files
Referential coverage of customer_id against the customer table fell to 91 percent
An optional field was added by the producer without breaking existing readers
The share of null-defaulted values in one device slice tripled

variants.hint: Partition completeness and referential coverage are not the same kind of claim.
variants.explanation: Boundaries stay independent so a compatible schema change is never confused with an incomplete or shifted dataset.
